name: Tech neck correction

lead: Tech neck, or text neck, is a popular name for a forward-leaning head posture linked to long hours on phones and laptops. Correction covers ergonomic changes, posture awareness and strengthening or stretching of neck and upper-back muscles.
In looksmaxxing circles, it is discussed as a way to improve neck length and jaw definition in profile. Published research looks at pain and posture, not at changes to appearance.

paras: Approaches described in clinical sources aim to strengthen deep neck flexors and scapular muscles, stretch tight posterior neck muscles, and reduce sustained screen-flexed positions with breaks and better screen height.

Posture exercises are generally described as low risk, though people with neck pain or neurological symptoms are usually advised by clinicians to seek assessment. Research on the topic is limited by the lack of a standard definition of text neck.

lead: Tech neck, also called text neck, is an informal name for a forward-leaning head and neck posture associated with prolonged use of phones, tablets and laptops, and for the discomfort sometimes attributed to it. "Tech neck correction" refers to the exercises, ergonomic changes and posture habits that people use to reduce that posture. In looksmaxxing culture it is discussed mainly as a posture topic, because forward head carriage is said to shorten the visual neck line and soften the jaw-to-neck transition.[1][2]

A 2023 scoping review of peer-reviewed articles found no consensus definition of text neck, which it described as a challenge for researchers and clinicians.[3] Related clinical literature on forward head posture links it to long device use and to neck and upper-back pain, though the strength of that association differs by age group.[1][4]

Evidence on appearance outcomes specifically is thin. Published work focuses on symptoms, posture measurement and skin changes on the neck, not on how posture correction alters facial or jaw appearance.
infobox: Ergonomics, posture awareness, strengthening and stretching exercises

paras: Wikipedia describes forward head posture as the head sitting ahead of the shoulders, commonly measured by the position of the ear relative to the shoulder, and links most cases to hours of hunching over laptops, tablets and phones. Occupations such as dentistry, surgery, hairdressing and desk work are also listed.[1] When combined with rounded shoulders the pattern is called upper crossed syndrome.[1]

"Tech neck" and "text neck" are popular terms rather than formal diagnoses. The 2023 scoping review searched five databases and reported that the terms are defined inconsistently across the literature.[3]

Sources on forward head posture describe strengthening of the deep neck flexors and scapular retractors, stretching of the upper trapezius, thoracic mobilization, regular breaks and ergonomic set-up as the usual approaches.[1] Several of these statements are marked as needing further confirmation on the Wikipedia page itself.[1]

A small 2024 study examined instrument-assisted soft tissue mobilization on specific muscles in people with tech neck.[5] A 2025 pilot questionnaire study in a work setting examined how ergonomic tools, break frequency and posture awareness related to symptom intensity.[6]

A 2023 open-label study in Chinese women used a topical cosmeceutical regimen aimed at "tech neck" lines, meaning skin creasing on the neck in younger people, a different use of the term from posture.[7] The study was single-centre and had no control group.

Studies to date mostly concern symptoms and posture rather than appearance. The 2023 scoping review addressed definitions only.[3] A 2025 cross-sectional pilot questionnaire explored symptoms and preventive measures.[6] A 2024 trial-style study examined soft tissue mobilization.[5] A 2019 meta-analysis cited on Wikipedia found a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents.[1] No published study found in this research has tested whether correcting tech neck changes jawline or facial appearance.

Posture is treated in these communities as part of overall presentation: proponents say upright head carriage makes the neck look longer and the jaw more defined, and that devices and desk habits are a common cause of a forward head. Specific exercises associated with this goal, such as chin tucks, are discussed in a separate article.

timeline.event: Hansraj publishes a widely cited analysis of cervical spine loading at different head-flexion angles, referenced in coverage of forward head posture.[1]
A meta-analysis reports a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not in adolescents.[1]
Scoping review finds no consensus definition of text neck.[3]
